chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Al-Husayn ibn Zur'arah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding the skin of a dead sheep that is tanned, milk and water are poured into it, so one drinks from it and performs ablution with it. He said: Yes. And he said: It is tanned and benefit is derived from it, and one prays in it. Al-Husayn said: And my father asked him about the udder that is in the belly of the she-camel and the goat, and it is dead, so he said: There is no harm in it.

key_terms.جِلْدِ شَاةٍ مَيِّتَةٍ: skin of a dead sheep (animal not ritually slaughtered)
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: there is no harm in it (permissible/pure)

ai.seo_question: Is the skin of an animal that died naturally pure and usable for prayer after tanning?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani’s al--Istibsar clarifies the status of *jild al-maytah* (skin of non-ritually slaughtered animals) through the chain of the Four Scholars, affirming that tanning (*dabgh*) purifies the hide, rendering it fit for use in prayer (*salat*) and ablution (*wudu*). It further extends this purity to the udders of camels and goats, resolving juristic debates on whether natural death renders the entire carcass impure or if specific parts retain purity through tanning or inherent nature.
